blocks.content: The previous topic ended on a deliberately unresolved thread: an Ingress object alone does nothing. This topic resolves that thread completely, covering the actual piece of software that turns declared routing rules into real, working traffic flow.
Ingress Controller, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Ingress Controller, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: An Ingress controller is a piece of software, running as ordinary Pods inside the cluster, that continuously watches for Ingress objects and configures a real HTTP proxy to actually implement the routing rules those objects declare.

Popular Ingress controller implementations include NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, and HAProxy Ingress, along with cloud specific implementations, each ultimately performing the same core job through a different underlying proxy technology.

Kubernetes ships the Ingress API object type as part of its core API, but deliberately does not ship any specific controller implementation by default, leaving the choice of implementation to whoever operates the cluster.

This separation between the API, what routing rules can be declared, and the controller, what software actually enforces them, is a deliberate design choice that gives cluster operators real flexibility in choosing the underlying technology.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643048770-637468436.png
blocks.alt: Ingress controller given its own full depth

blocks.content: An Ingress Object Alone Does Nothing
blocks.text: An Ingress Object Alone Does Nothing

blocks.content: This is worth restating plainly, exactly as the previous topic's common mistake section demonstrated: creating an Ingress object with kubectl apply succeeds at the API level regardless of whether any controller exists to act on it.

The Ingress object is stored in etcd exactly like any other Kubernetes object, fully valid and fully queryable, but with genuinely zero effect on real network traffic until some controller is actively watching for it and reacting.

This is precisely the same declarative intent versus active reconciliation pattern already covered for Deployments, Services, and LoadBalancer provisioning throughout this entire course, applied here to HTTP routing specifically.

Understanding this pattern as a recurring theme, rather than a surprising exception specific to Ingress, is what makes this particular gap easy to anticipate and diagnose quickly rather than a confusing new category of problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643050423-448257169.png
blocks.alt: An Ingress object alone does nothing without a controller

blocks.content: A Real Ingress Controller Installation

Installing the NGINX Ingress Controller, the most widely used implementation, typically involves applying a set of manifests provided by the project, which creates a Deployment running the controller's Pods along with its own supporting Service.

Once installed and running, the controller begins watching the cluster's Ingress objects immediately, and any existing Ingress manifests that were previously sitting inert begin working correctly within moments, without needing to be recreated or modified.

The controller's own Service is typically type LoadBalancer, provisioning exactly the one external cloud load balancer described in the previous topic, which then becomes the single external entry point for every application routed through Ingress.

This single installation step is genuinely the only piece of extra setup required. From that point forward, every Ingress object created on the cluster is automatically picked up and enforced without any further controller level configuration.

# A typical NGINX Ingress Controller installation
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml

# Confirm it is running
kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx

blocks.content: Recap: The General Controller Pattern

The Kubernetes Architecture module introduced the controller pattern in general terms: watch the API server for a desired state, compare it to the real world, and take action to close any gap between the two, continuously and automatically.

The Controller Manager topic in that same module gave several concrete built in examples of this pattern already running inside the control plane by default, such as the ReplicaSet controller and the Endpoints controller covered later in this course.

An Ingress controller is precisely one more instance of this exact same pattern, with one meaningful difference: it is not built into the control plane by default, and must instead be deliberately installed as its own separate workload.

Recognizing an Ingress controller as another concrete example of a pattern already deeply familiar from earlier in this course removes any sense of it being a fundamentally new or unusual kind of component.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643053703-84974479.png
blocks.alt: Recap of the general controller pattern

blocks.content: Running as Ordinary Pods Behind a Real Entry Point
blocks.text: Running as Ordinary Pods Behind a Real Entry Point

blocks.content: An Ingress controller's own Pods are entirely ordinary from Kubernetes's perspective: they can be scaled with replicas, monitored with the exact same kubectl commands, and replaced automatically by a ReplicaSet if one happens to fail.

This means every resilience concept covered throughout this course, self healing, rolling updates, resource requests and limits, applies directly and without exception to the Ingress controller itself, exactly as it would to any other application.

The controller's own exposure to external traffic, most commonly through a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service in front of it, is precisely the layering pattern already established in the previous module: ClusterIP, then NodePort, then LoadBalancer, now with an Ingress controller sitting behind that entry point.
Seeing the Ingress controller as simply another application, deployed and exposed using tools already fully understood from earlier in this course, is the key to demystifying it entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643055378-294626794.png
blocks.alt: An Ingress controller running as ordinary Pods behind a load balancer

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Assuming a Default Controller Exists
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Assuming a Default Controller Exists

blocks.content: A common mistake, especially among engineers moving from a fully managed platform as a service environment to a raw Kubernetes cluster, is assuming every cluster ships with a working Ingress controller installed and ready by default.

Some managed cloud Kubernetes offerings do bundle a default Ingress controller as a convenience, but this is a platform specific choice, not a Kubernetes core guarantee, and it should never be assumed true without explicitly verifying it.

The correct first step on any new or unfamiliar cluster, before writing a single Ingress manifest, is running kubectl get pods across all namespaces and looking specifically for an existing Ingress controller Deployment already present and running.

If none exists, installing one, as demonstrated earlier in this topic, is a mandatory prerequisite, not an optional enhancement, before any Ingress object created afterward can have any real effect on traffic at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643056924-475736398.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of assuming every cluster has an Ingress controller by default

blocks.content: Choosing Between Ingress Controller Implementations

NGINX Ingress Controller is the most widely adopted implementation, backed by a large community, extensive documentation, and broad compatibility across nearly every cloud and on premises environment, making it a genuinely safe default choice for most teams.

Traefik offers a more dynamic, automatically reloading configuration model and strong integration with modern service mesh and certificate automation tooling, appealing particularly to teams already invested in its broader ecosystem.

Cloud specific Ingress controllers, such as AWS Load Balancer Controller, integrate more tightly with their specific cloud provider's native load balancing features, at the cost of being less portable to a different cloud or an on premises environment.

For most teams starting out, NGINX Ingress Controller remains the pragmatic default, with a switch to a more specialized implementation reserved for cases with a specific, well understood requirement the default does not satisfy.

Watching the Controller Do Its Job
blocks.text: Watching the Controller Do Its Job

blocks.content: Once an Ingress controller is installed, its logs, viewed with kubectl logs against its Pods in the ingress-nginx namespace or wherever it was installed, show every Ingress object it discovers and every configuration reload it performs in response.

Applying a new Ingress manifest and immediately tailing the controller's logs is a genuinely useful, hands on way to build confidence that the controller is actually watching and reacting, rather than simply trusting that it works invisibly.

Most controller implementations also expose their own internal configuration state through a debug endpoint or a dedicated status command, letting an engineer inspect exactly how a given set of Ingress rules was translated into real proxy configuration.

Building this habit of directly observing the controller's behavior, rather than only observing the end result at the application level, pays off significantly the first time a routing rule does not behave as expected.
Controller Resource Sizing in Production

Because every single piece of external HTTP traffic for every application behind it passes through the Ingress controller, its own resource requests, limits, and replica count deserve the same careful production sizing attention as any other high traffic, business critical component.

An under resourced Ingress controller becomes a genuine, cluster wide bottleneck, since a slowdown there affects every single application routed through it simultaneously, unlike an under resourced individual application Pod, which only affects itself.

Most production deployments run the Ingress controller with multiple replicas for both capacity and resilience, exactly the same ReplicaSet backed scaling pattern already fully covered in the Deployments and Replication modules earlier in this course.

Monitoring the Ingress controller's own resource usage and request latency as a distinct, first class metric, separate from any individual application's own metrics, is a genuinely important operational practice in any real production cluster.

blocks.title: Operational Note
blocks.content: The Ingress controller sits in front of every HTTP application in the cluster. Size and monitor it with the same seriousness given to any single point of entry for production traffic.
Multiple Ingress Controllers on One Cluster
blocks.text: Multiple Ingress Controllers on One Cluster

blocks.content: It is possible, and occasionally useful, to run more than one Ingress controller on the same cluster, for example separating internal, private traffic from external, public traffic through two entirely distinct controllers and entry points.

The ingressClassName field on an Ingress object specifies which of several installed controllers should handle that specific object's rules, giving a clean, explicit way to direct different applications to different controllers deliberately.

Without this field set explicitly, an Ingress object is handled by whichever controller is configured as the cluster's default, which can lead to unexpected behavior on a cluster running more than one controller without careful configuration.

This multi controller pattern is an advanced setup, not needed by most teams, but understanding it exists is useful for correctly interpreting the ingressClassName field when it appears in a real world manifest.
Upgrading an Ingress Controller Safely

Because every application routed through Ingress depends on the controller, upgrading it to a new version deserves the same careful, staged rollout discipline already covered for application Deployments in earlier modules of this course.

Most Ingress controller Deployments support the exact same rolling update strategy already fully covered for ordinary applications, replacing old controller Pods with new ones gradually, while readiness probes ensure traffic only shifts to Pods that are genuinely ready.

Testing a controller upgrade against a small, non critical subset of routed traffic first, where practical, is a genuinely valuable extra safety step given how much of a cluster's external traffic depends on this one component functioning correctly.

Reviewing the specific release notes for any Ingress controller version upgrade is also worth the small time investment, since breaking changes to annotation names or default behaviors do occasionally occur between major versions.
Ingress Controller Observability

Beyond the basic log tailing already covered, most Ingress controller implementations expose Prometheus compatible metrics directly, covering request counts, latencies, and error rates broken down by which Ingress rule or backend Service handled each request.

These metrics are genuinely valuable for building a cluster wide traffic dashboard, since the Ingress controller sees every single piece of external HTTP traffic passing through the cluster, making it an unusually rich single source of observability data.

Setting up alerting on Ingress controller error rates and latency, distinct from any individual application's own metrics, catches problems that manifest specifically at the routing layer, such as a misconfigured rule or an overwhelmed backend, before they are noticed elsewhere.

This observability layer connects directly to the Observability module covered later in this course, where metrics collection and alerting are given their own full, dedicated treatment beyond this specific Ingress controller context.
A Real World Controller Failure Scenario
blocks.text: A Real World Controller Failure Scenario

blocks.content: Consider a cluster where the Ingress controller's own Pods, running with only a single replica, encounter an out of memory condition under an unexpected traffic spike, causing the one running Pod to be terminated and restarted.

During the brief window before the replacement Pod becomes ready, every single application routed through that Ingress controller becomes simultaneously unreachable, a considerably larger blast radius than a single application's own Pod failing would ever cause.

Running the Ingress controller with multiple replicas, exactly as recommended in the resource sizing section earlier in this topic, directly prevents this scenario, since remaining healthy replicas continue serving traffic while any one replica recovers.

This scenario is a concrete, memorable illustration of why the earlier resource sizing and replica count guidance is not a theoretical best practice, but a direct, practical defense against a real, observed failure mode in production clusters.

blocks.title: Real World Lesson
blocks.content: A single replica Ingress controller is a single point of failure for every application behind it. Multiple replicas are not optional polish, they are a direct defense against a real, observed failure mode.
The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

The Ingress controller is the missing piece that makes every Ingress object covered in the previous topic actually work. Without it installed and running, Ingress rules are declared intent with zero real effect on traffic.

Installing one, most commonly NGINX Ingress Controller for a first production deployment, is a mandatory, deliberate step, never a safe assumption, and verifying its presence should be an early check on any unfamiliar cluster.

The next topic, Path Based Routing, covers the first of the two core routing mechanisms an installed controller actually enforces, building directly on the manifest structure already introduced in the previous topic.

Keep the controller pattern firmly in mind: Ingress objects declare intent, and the controller, running as ordinary Pods, continuously reconciles real proxy configuration to match that intent, exactly like every other controller covered throughout this course.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: verifying an Ingress controller's presence and health takes thirty seconds and belongs at the very start of any unfamiliar cluster investigation, well before writing a single Ingress rule.

With the controller now fully understood, the next two topics can focus entirely on the routing rules themselves, confident that the machinery actually enforcing them has already been covered in complete depth.
Module Seven continues directly from here into path based routing, the first of those two rule mechanisms.

blocks.title: Ingress Controller In Full
points: An Ingress controller is software, running as ordinary Pods, that watches Ingress objects and configures a real HTTP proxy to enforce their routing rules.
Kubernetes ships the Ingress API but no default controller implementation; installing one, such as NGINX Ingress Controller, is a mandatory prerequisite, not an optional convenience.
It is another concrete instance of the general controller pattern already covered throughout this course, applied specifically to HTTP routing.
Because it fronts every application behind it, its own resource sizing, replica count, and monitoring deserve production grade attention.
Path Based Routing, covered next, is the first of the two core routing mechanisms an installed Ingress controller actually enforces.
